title: Why real-world data matters for AI
summary: Regional accents, overlapping speech and phone audio are part of the conditions an AI product has to work in — and often missing from the datasets models train on.
body_markdown:
Real-world data is noisy, inconsistent and full of details that often get filtered out of a clean dataset. But those details can be exactly what a model needs to learn: a regional accent, two people interrupting each other, the sound of a voice through a cheap phone. They are part of the conditions an AI product has to work in. At Luel, we collect real-world data to bring more of those conditions into training, especially where existing datasets leave people out.


## What the available data leaves out


A language can have millions of speakers and very little recorded, transcribed speech. Even where recordings exist, they may capture a narrow version of the language: formal broadcasts, prepared sentences, a handful of speakers reading aloud. More hours of that material can leave everyday conversation just as poorly represented.


People use different vocabulary when they speak freely. They shorten words, switch languages and pronounce the same phrase differently across regions. A model needs examples of those patterns to learn how the language is used beyond a script. For a voice product, that difference affects whose speech it can understand and how naturally it can speak back.


This is part of the reason Luel builds native-speaker corpora for Masri, Darija, Tibetan and Dzongkha. Each brings its own collection needs, from spoken Arabic dialects to languages with little available training material. Working directly with native speakers lets us build around the language we intend to serve.


## What real recordings make possible


The benefit goes beyond representing more speakers. Recordings from different devices and environments give a model examples of how the same task changes in practice. A request still needs transcribing when someone moves away from the microphone. A conversation still needs separating when speakers interrupt each other.


Real-world data also changes how a model should be judged. Open language identifiers are mostly built and scored on clean, scripted, studio-read audio, and that is what the public leaderboards measure. Our contributors record on phones, in real rooms and in real conversation. So we built[Luel Language ID](https://www.luel.ai/lab/models/language-id) for that audio, and we judge it on whether it knows when to answer.


Our language-ID specialty is selective prediction: coverage at a held accuracy, with abstention when the system does not have enough evidence to answer — not a claim to be the most accurate language identifier. When a clip is too short or too narrow-band to call, the model declines instead of guessing. The method is set out in[Duration-Resolved LID](https://www.luel.ai/lab/benchmarks/duration-resolved-lid) .


A team building for phone recordings needs to know how a model handles phone recordings. Collecting that audio makes the gap visible and gives researchers something concrete to improve against.


## Why useful data is still missing


The conversations already happen. Turning them into usable data takes work: finding the right speakers, arranging consent, recording the relevant conditions and checking what was submitted. A regional expression needs someone who understands it. Overlapping speech needs careful annotation. Those requirements make some of the most useful data difficult to collect at scale.


Quality control is part of that process. An accurate transcript of a noisy recording can be valuable; a wrong transcript teaches the wrong thing. The task also decides what to keep. For a system that has to handle interruptions, the overlap is the point, and cleaning it out would remove what the model needs to learn.


At Luel, more than 900,000 contributors across 96+ countries record audio, video and images, and every speech submission runs through quality assurance before anything downstream can use it. That gives us a way to reach communities and conditions that existing datasets miss, then turn their contributions into data a model can use.


Synthetic data can expand the scenarios we already understand. Real-world collection helps us discover what is missing and measure whether a system works for the people using it. That is why we keep collecting: every new language, community and setting gives us a more complete picture of what our models need to learn.
